Module 01 · Foundations

Introduction to Inferential Statistics

Statistics splits into two jobs: describing data you already have, and inferring things about data you don't. This module builds the mental model you'll use for every topic that follows.

Descriptive vs. Inferential

📊 Descriptive statistics

Summarizes the data you actually collected. Mean, median, charts, tables — no guessing beyond what's in front of you.

🔭 Inferential statistics

Uses a sample to make a justified guess about a population you can't fully observe — with a stated level of confidence and uncertainty.

Why it matters in business: You can't survey every customer, test every product unit, or wait for every user to churn. Inferential statistics lets you act on a sample of 500 and speak responsibly about millions.

Population vs. Sample — the core vocabulary

ILLUSTRATION

A population of 2,000,000 (gray) vs. a sample of 500 (teal) drawn from it — the sample statistic estimates the population parameter.

Key vocabulary you'll use throughout

Parameter

A number describing the whole population (μ, σ, p). Usually unknown — that's the whole problem.

Statistic

A number computed from a sample (x̄, s, p̂). Known, and used to estimate the parameter.

Estimate

A statistic's best guess at the parameter, always reported with a margin of error.

The roadmap ahead

Every later module is one piece of the same pipeline:

population ──sample──▶ data ──model──▶ probability ──estimate──▶ confidence interval ──test──▶ decision
  • Probability & Bayes — the rules that let us reason about uncertainty.
  • Distributions — the shapes uncertain outcomes tend to take.
  • Sampling & CI — how a sample statistic relates to the true parameter.
  • Hypothesis testing — turning evidence into a yes/no decision, responsibly.
  • Correlation — reading relationships between variables without fooling yourself.
Module 02 · Probability Foundations

Random Variables & Conditional Probability

A random variable turns an uncertain outcome into a number. Conditional probability updates our belief once we learn new information. Both are the plumbing behind every statistical test you'll ever run.

Random variables: discrete vs. continuous

🎲 Discrete

Countable outcomes: number of defective units, customer support tickets per day, heads in 10 coin flips.

📏 Continuous

Any value in a range: delivery time in minutes, customer height, transaction amount.

ILLUSTRATION

Rolling two dice enough times traces out this exact theoretical distribution — a random variable's distribution is simply its long-run pattern of outcomes.

Conditional probability

The probability of A given that B already happened. Learning B shrinks the space of possible outcomes to only those consistent with B.

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
ILLUSTRATION

Conditioning on “red card” shrinks the sample space from 52 cards to 26 — every probability you compute afterward is relative to that smaller space.

Independence — the special case

A and B are independent if knowing B tells you nothing new about A: P(A|B) = P(A). This is rarer in real business data than people assume — marketing channel and purchase, weather and footfall, and device type and conversion are all usually dependent.

Common trap: treating correlated events (e.g. "used mobile app" and "made repeat purchase") as independent when computing joint probabilities — this silently overstates or understates risk in models.
Module 02 · Probability Foundations

Bayes' Theorem & Real-world Bayes

Bayes' theorem is how a rational mind updates a belief after seeing evidence. It's also the single most misread piece of math in medicine, spam filtering, and fraud detection — usually because people ignore the base rate.

The formula

P(A | B) = [ P(B | A) · P(A) ] / P(B)
  • P(A) — the prior: what we believed before any evidence (the base rate).
  • P(B|A) — the likelihood: how probable the evidence is if A is true.
  • P(A|B) — the posterior: our updated belief after seeing evidence B.

Real-world Bayes #1 — the medical test paradox

ILLUSTRATION

Even with a 99%-accurate test, a rare disease means most positive results are false alarms — only 1 of the 6 positive results here is a true positive.

Takeaway: when a condition is rare, most positive results are false positives — even with a "95%–99% accurate" test. Always ask: what's the base rate?

Real-world Bayes #2 — spam filter

ILLUSTRATION

Each spam-associated word shifts the probability further from the prior — this is exactly how a Naive Bayes spam filter reasons.

Where else Bayes shows up in business

Fraud detection

Base rate of fraud is tiny (~0.1%) — flag thresholds must account for overwhelming false positives.

A/B test monitoring

Bayesian A/B testing updates "probability B beats A" continuously as data arrives.

Churn scoring

Behavioral signals (support tickets, login gaps) update a prior churn probability per customer.

Module 03 · Distributions

Normal, Binomial & Poisson Distributions

A probability distribution is a "shape" that tells you which outcomes are likely. Most business randomness fits one of three shapes below — knowing which one to reach for is the real skill.

Normal distribution — the bell curve

Symmetric, continuous, defined by mean μ and standard deviation σ. Heights, measurement errors, and — thanks to the Central Limit Theorem — almost any average, all tend to look normal.

ILLUSTRATION

The classic bell curve: about 68% of values sit within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.

The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% of values fall within 1σ of μ, 95% within 2σ, and 99.7% within 3σ. Drag the sliders and watch the shaded region track this.

Binomial distribution — counting successes

Counts the number of successes in n independent yes/no trials, each with success probability p. Think: conversions out of 100 visitors, defective items out of a batch.

ILLUSTRATION

20 trials at a 30% success rate — the distribution peaks near the expected count (np = 6) and tapers off on either side.

Poisson distribution — counting rare events over time

Counts events in a fixed interval when events happen independently at an average rate λ. Think: support tickets per hour, website crashes per day, machine failures per month.

ILLUSTRATION

With an average of 4 events per interval, most intervals see 2–6 events — rare intervals can still spike much higher.

Choosing the right distribution for a business problem

Is your outcome a count of successes out of a fixed, known number of trials? (e.g. 40 conversions out of 500 emails sent)
→ Use Binomial
Is your outcome a count of events over time/space with no fixed upper limit? (e.g. server errors per hour)
→ Use Poisson
Is your outcome a continuous measurement, or an average/sum of many small effects? (e.g. delivery time, average order value)
→ Use Normal
Rule of thumb: Binomial answers "how many out of n?", Poisson answers "how many in this stretch of time?", Normal answers "what does the average/measurement look like?"
Module 04 · Sampling & Estimation

Sampling Techniques & the Central Limit Theorem

You'll never measure an entire population, so how you pick a sample decides whether your conclusions are trustworthy — and the CLT is why sample averages behave so predictably.

Sampling techniques

ILLUSTRATION

Four ways to choose who gets surveyed — each trades off representativeness, cost, and ease of implementation differently.

Simple random

Every unit has equal chance of selection — the gold standard, but needs a full list of the population.

Systematic

Pick every k-th unit from a list (e.g. every 10th customer). Easy to implement, risky if the list has hidden patterns.

Stratified

Split into subgroups (e.g. region, age band) and sample proportionally from each — guarantees representation.

Cluster

Split into clusters (e.g. stores), randomly pick whole clusters, and survey everyone inside them — cheaper logistically.

The Central Limit Theorem

Claim: no matter how skewed the original population is, the distribution of sample means becomes approximately Normal as sample size n grows — usually by n ≈ 30.

ILLUSTRATION

Even though the original population (left) is heavily skewed, the distribution of sample means becomes bell-shaped as sample size grows (right) — the Central Limit Theorem in action.

Standard Error — how precise is the sample mean?

SE = σ / √n

Standard Error measures how much sample means bounce around the true population mean. Notice the square root: to halve your error, you need 4× the sample size — not 2×. This is why "just collect a bit more data" often disappoints.

Module 04 · Sampling & Estimation

Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval turns a single-number estimate into an honest range, and states how sure we are it captures the truth.

What does "95% CI" actually mean?

Not this: "There's a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval." The true mean is fixed, not random — it either is or isn't in any single interval.
Actually this: "If we repeated this sampling process many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean."
ILLUSTRATION

Each horizontal line is a 95% confidence interval from an independent experiment. The ones in red missed the true population mean purely by chance — that's what “95% confidence” means over the long run.

Computing a CI: z-score vs. t-distribution method

z-method

Use when population σ is known, or n is large (≥30). Uses the standard normal z critical value.

t-method

Use when σ is unknown and estimated from the sample (the usual real-world case), especially with small n. Uses the t-distribution, which has fatter tails to account for extra uncertainty.

CI = x̄ ± (critical value) × SE   where SE = s/√n
ILLUSTRATION

A confidence interval reports a range, not a single number — this one spans the estimate ± its margin of error.

Margin of Error

Margin of Error = (critical value) × SE

The "±3%" you see quoted in political polls is the margin of error. Widening your confidence level (95% → 99%) or shrinking your sample both inflate it. Notice: it's exactly the number you add/subtract from the estimate above to get the CI.

Module 05 · Hypothesis Testing

Null vs. Alternate Hypothesis & T-tests

Hypothesis testing is the formal way to ask "could this result have happened just by chance?" — and decide, with a clear rulebook, when to believe it didn't.

Null (H₀) vs Alternate (H₁)

H₀ — Null hypothesis

The "boring" default: no effect, no difference, no relationship. e.g. "The new checkout flow has the same conversion rate as the old one."

H₁ — Alternate hypothesis

What you suspect is true and want evidence for. e.g. "The new checkout flow has a different conversion rate."

We never "prove" H₀ or H₁ true. We ask: if H₀ were true, how surprising would this data be? If very surprising (small p-value), we reject H₀.

p-values, significance, and the two errors

Type I error (α)

Rejecting H₀ when it was actually true — a "false alarm." α (often 0.05) is the risk you accept.

Type II error (β)

Failing to reject H₀ when H₁ was actually true — a "missed effect."

T-test — comparing means

A t-test checks whether the difference between two group means is bigger than you'd expect from random sampling noise alone.

ILLUSTRATION

Two overlapping distributions with different means — a t-test asks whether that gap is bigger than random sampling noise would produce.

Notice: the same mean difference can be "significant" or "not significant" purely depending on sample size and spread. A bigger n makes small true differences detectable — significance is not the same as importance.
Module 05 · Hypothesis Testing

Chi-square, ANOVA & A/B Testing

Once you move past comparing two means, you need tools for categories (chi-square), more than two groups (ANOVA), and the everyday business version of all of this: A/B testing.

Chi-square test — are two categorical variables related?

Compares observed counts in a table against what you'd expect if the variables were independent.

χ² = Σ (Observed − Expected)² / Expected
ILLUSTRATION

Comparing observed counts across categories — a chi-square test checks whether the pattern differs from what independence would predict.

ANOVA — comparing more than two group means

Analysis of Variance asks: is the variation between group means bigger than the variation within groups? If yes, at least one group differs.

F = Variance between groups / Variance within groups
ILLUSTRATION

Three groups, three means — ANOVA tests whether the spread between group means is bigger than the natural spread within each group.

A/B testing — hypothesis testing in production

An A/B test is a two-sample test (often on conversion rates) run live on real users. Same statistical machinery as above, just applied to proportions.

ILLUSTRATION

A meaningful lift in conversion rate, tested for statistical significance before rolling out to everyone.

Module 06 · Relationships in Data

Correlation & Business Statistics

Correlation measures how two variables move together. It's one of the most useful — and most abused — tools in business analytics.

Pearson vs. Spearman

Pearson (r)

Measures linear relationship strength between two continuous variables. Sensitive to outliers.

Spearman (ρ)

Measures monotonic relationship using ranks instead of raw values — works for non-linear-but-consistent trends, and is outlier-resistant.

ILLUSTRATION

Correlation strength ranges from strong and linear to nonexistent — and a single outlier (right panel) can swing Pearson's r dramatically.

Correlation vs. Causation

Ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths. Does ice cream cause drowning? No — both rise with hot weather. A hidden confounding variable (temperature) drives both.
Live demo · Spot the confounder
Pick a scenario

Business-stats checklist before you trust a correlation

  • Is there a plausible mechanism, or could a third variable (time, seasonality, size) explain both?
  • Does the relationship hold in a randomized experiment, not just observational data?
  • Is the correlation driven by a handful of outliers? (Compare Pearson vs Spearman.)
  • Would reverse causation make just as much sense? (Does revenue drive headcount, or headcount drive revenue?)
